context: Current closing price of iShares Russell 2000 (IWM): $301.40 USD as of 2026-08-19.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I interpreted as a current price level near $301–302, with the 1-day estimate of $302.1 essentially anchoring near the prevailing price given that very little should change in a single session under baseline conditions. The 1-week estimate of $303.5 incorporates a small positive drift consistent with the long-run average daily return of broad equity indices, assuming no major macro disruptions. The 1-month estimate of $306 extends that same drift logic further out, implying roughly a 1.3% gain over the month, which is modest but in line with historical average monthly returns for something like the S&P 500 or a similar index-linked instrument. In all three cases, I was not assuming any strong directional catalyst, just mean-drift behavior under normal market conditions.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily using historical volatility as the key input. For the 1-day window, realized daily volatility for large-cap equity indices tends to run around 1–1.5%, which maps closely to the roughly ±2% band I applied. For the 1-week horizon, uncertainty compounds with the square root of time, so the interval widens to roughly ±5%, and at 1 month it expands further to around ±10–11%. These widths also reflect the fact that equity markets can exhibit volatility clustering — quiet periods can be interrupted by sudden spikes — so I tried to avoid intervals that were too tight even if recent realized vol had been subdued.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise Federal Reserve policy shift, either an emergency rate cut or unexpected hawkishness, which historically has caused single-day moves of 3–5% or more. Geopolitical escalation, a credit event in a major financial institution, or a significant inflation data surprise could similarly produce tail moves. On the upside, a sudden de-escalation of trade tensions, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, or a dovish pivot could drive prices well above $338 over a month.

It's also worth acknowledging structural uncertainty in my forecast: I don't have access to real-time market data, so my starting price anchor may itself be imprecise. If the actual current price differs meaningfully from my assumed baseline, all three point estimates would shift accordingly, and the intervals would need to be recentered. This epistemic uncertainty about the starting condition is arguably as important as the stochastic uncertainty embedded in the interval widths themselves.
